extracted.intended_audience: general readers and mathematicians interested in the foundations and history of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Expository treatment of foundational issues in mathematics (logic vs intuition), the nature and legitimacy of mathematical proof (especially mathematical induction), and the historical development and role of symbolic notation in algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of sound reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: To reason soundly one must first define premises without ambiguity, then apply the rules of logic step-by-step to arrive at a conclusion which is the unique consequence of the logical process used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the conclusion disagrees with observed facts first check whether the rules of logic were applied correctly; if they were, then inspect premises for inconsistency or mismatch to the concrete problem. The laws of reasoning are the skeleton of intellect and underlie deductive mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatic system desiderata
rubrics_metrics.description: An acceptable set of assumptions (axioms/postulates) should be free from contradiction, have each assumption independent of the others, and be exhaustive (completely cover the question under investigation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing such a set requires acute analytic judgment and skill; the branch of mathematics addressing these problems is axiomatics (e.g., work of Peano, Russell, Hilbert). These properties matter because arithmetic's properties depend on the chosen axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive method (mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical reasoning proceeds deductively: start from very general properties (definitions, postulates, axioms) and derive particular statements by rules of logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deduction is the basis of mathematical proof and distinguishes mathematics from empirical sciences. Geometry historically served as the model of deductive structure for exact sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical induction inadmissible in mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of induction as used in experimental sciences (generalizing from repeated observations) is barred from rigorous mathematics; evidence from any number of cases is insufficient to prove a general mathematical proposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single counterexample suffices to disprove a mathematical assertion. Examples include polynomial expressions that produce primes for many initial inputs but fail later; thus physical-style induction is unacceptable as proof in arithmetic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical induction (reasoning by recurrence) — two necessary steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete mathematical induction (reasoning by recurrence) requires (1) a base case showing the proposition true for the first term and (2) the hereditary/induction step showing that truth for an arbitrary term implies truth for its successor; both steps are necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by proving associativity of addition: show the proposition for c = 1 (base) and prove that truth for c = n implies truth for c = n+1 (hereditary). Historical notes: Pascal formulated the principle; Bertrand Russell's term 'hereditary' used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restricted vs. general principle of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The restricted principle (a finite chain of syllogisms) is a consequence of classical logic and suffices for a bounded/finite arithmetic; the general (complete) principle asserts validity for an indefinite/infinite sequence and tacitly assumes every number has a successor (an assertion not derivable from classical logic or experience).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restricted induction can yield a logically impregnable finite arithmetic (e.g., ending counting at a million), but the general principle requires acceptance of the infinite and is a mathematical necessity not imposed by logic or empirical observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability condition for mathematical induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical induction is applicable only when the same operation or process can be repeated indefinitely (i.e., the sequence has successors ad infinitum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If operations are not indefinitely repeatable (e.g., chess moves that do not resemble one another), induction cannot produce a science. The ability to conceive indefinite repetition is a faculty of the mind, distinct from empirical induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of mathematical truth via non-contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical proposition is true if it leads to no logical contradiction, and false otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This embodies the principle of contradiction as the foundation of deductive mathematical proof: truth is established by demonstrating absence of contradiction within the logical framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof verification procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a deductive conclusion conflicts with observation, two possibilities must be checked: (a) whether the rules of logic were applied correctly, and (b) whether the premises are inconsistent or inappropriate for the concrete problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rules were applied correctly but the conclusion fails to match facts, it's the assumptions ('the fitter of the suit') at fault rather than the logical tailoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and necessity of symbolism in algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic notation is essential to algebra: symbols permit abstraction from concrete perception, turning objects into operands for formal operations; without symbols algebra cannot develop fully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical argument: rhetorical algebra (words) and syncopated algebra (abbreviations) preceded symbolic algebra. The symbol is not mere formality but the essence of algebra; symbolic notation enabled modern algebraic operations and advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of algebraic notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Algebra historically passed through three stages: rhetorical (full verbal form), syncopated (abbreviations of frequent words), and symbolic (independent symbols used operationally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each stage is characterized: rhetorical uses words symbolically; syncopated abbreviations can lose origin and become symbols; symbolic notation uses letters and signs to represent general magnitudes and operations (e.g., +, −, =).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design criteria for effective symbolic notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbolic conventions should be permanent in nature and clear to understand (distinguish given magnitudes from unknowns), offer economy of expression, and facilitate abstraction and manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vieta's vowel/consonant proposal to distinguish unknowns/givens; Descartes' Cartesian notation (first letters for given, last for unknown) became standard. Notation's economy (conciseness) aids thought even if initially radical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical caution about symbolism adoption
rubrics_metrics.description: Innovations in notation may appear merely formal but can be revolutionary; failure to adopt effective notation can retard development; conversely, notation should be evaluated for clarity and utility rather than dismissed as mere shorthand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated historically: Diophantus, Arabs, Hindus, Vieta, Descartes — different cultures progressed at different rates in adopting symbolic methods; successful notation often becomes habitual and appears 'natural' later.
